wiki_excerpt:
Pinus halepensis, commonly known as the Aleppo pine, also known as the Jerusalem pine, is a species of conifer in the family Pinaceae, a pine native to the Mediterranean region. It was officially named by the botanist Philip Miller in his 1768 book The Gardener's Dictionary; he probably never went to Aleppo but mentions seeing large specimens at Goodwood in the garden of the Duke of Richmond, which were transplanted (perhaps sent by Alexander Russell from Syria) in 1739.


Description
Pinus halepensis is a small to medium-sized tree, 15–25 metres (49–82 feet) tall, with a trunk diameter up to 60 centimetres (24 inches), exceptionally up to 1 m (3 ft 3 in). The bark is orange-red, thick, and deeply fissured at the base of the trunk, and thin and flaky in the upper crown. The leaves ('needles') are very slender, 6–12 cm (2+1⁄4–4+3⁄4 in) long, distinctly yellowish green, and produced in pairs (rarely a few in threes). The cones are narrow conic, 5–12 cm (2–4+3⁄4 in) long and 2–3 cm (3⁄4–1+1⁄4 in) broad at the base when closed, green at first, ripening glossy red-brown when 24 months old. They open slowly over the next few years, a process quickened if they are exposed to heat such as in forest fires. The cones open 5–8 cm (2–3+1⁄4 in) wide to allow the seeds to disperse. The seeds are 5–6 millimetres (3⁄16–1⁄4 in) long, with a 20 mm (13⁄16 in) wing, and are wind-dispersed.


Related species
The Aleppo pine is closely related to the Turkish pine, Canary Island pine, and maritime pine, which all share many of its characteristics. Some authors include the Turkish pine as a subspecies of the Aleppo pine, as Pinus halepensis subsp. brutia (Ten.) Holmboe, but it is usually regarded as a distinct species. It is a relatively nonvariable species, in that its morphological characteristics stay constant over the entire range.


Distribution and habitat
The native range of Pinus halepensis extends from Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Spain north to southern France, Malta, Italy, Croatia,  Montenegro, and Albania, and east to Greece. It has been introduced into many parts of the world, including Portugal. There is an outlying population (from which it was first described) in Syria, Lebanon, southern Turkey, Jordan, Israel and Palestine.
The species is generally found at low altitudes, mostly from sea level to 200 m (660 ft), but can grow above 1,000 m (3,300 ft) in southern and eastern Spain, well over 1,200 m (3,900 ft) on Crete, and up to 1,700 m (5,600 ft) in the south, in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
The tree is able to colonise open and disturbed areas quickly. It is classed as an invasive species in South Africa. It can grow on all substrates and almost in all bioclimates in the Mediterranean.
Pinus halepensis is a diagnostic species of the vegetation class Pinetea halepensis.


Uses


Local cuisines
The resin of the Aleppo pine is used to flavour the Greek wine retsina.

grok_lead: Pinus halepensis, commonly known as the Aleppo pine or Jerusalem pine, is a medium-sized evergreen conifer species belonging to the family Pinaceae, native to the Mediterranean region including countries such as Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, and North African nations like Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. This tree is characterized by its fast growth rate and adaptation to arid environments, typically reaching heights of 15â25 meters (50â82 feet) with a diameter at breast height up to 150 cm, featuring a single straight trunk that often branches low to form a broad, rounded or flat-topped crown. The bark is initially silvery-gray and smooth, becoming thick, fissured, and purple-brown with age, while the needles occur in pairs, measuring 5â12 cm long, slender, twisted, and grayish-green in color. The species produces ovoid to conical seed cones that are 6â12 cm long and 4â7 cm wide, maturing to a light brown color over three years and remaining on the branches for several years; these cones are armed with thick, slightly reflexed prickles. Native to coastal and inland areas of the Mediterranean Basin and western Asia, P. halepensis thrives in poor, dry, sandy or rocky soils and is highly drought-tolerant, with a hardiness extending to USDA Zone 8 (withstanding temperatures down to -12Â°C). It has been widely introduced outside its native range, including in California, South Africa, Australia, and parts of South America, where it is valued for reforestation, erosion control, and ornamental planting but can become invasive in some ecosystems due to its prolific seed production and fire resilience. Ecologically, Pinus halepensis plays a significant role in Mediterranean ecosystems, often dominating post-fire landscapes as its serotinous cones release seeds in response to heat, promoting rapid regeneration. The tree is economically important for timber, resin extraction, fuelwood, and as a source of pine honey from its abundant flowers, with mature specimens capable of living over 150 years. In regions like California, it is commonly referred to as the "freeway pine" due to its frequent use in urban landscaping along highways. Despite its utility, the species faces threats from climate change, pests, and habitat fragmentation in its native range, though it is currently assessed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.
